intro: The first movement of the Second Symphony, “Resurrection”, is an Allegro maestoso in C minor in the manner of a funeral march. Cellos and double basses open it under tremolo upper strings, and a long violin melody in E major returns several times over the course of the movement.

sections.label: A · March theme in cellos and basses
sections.mNote: Cellos and basses play beneath tremolo violins

sections.label: B · E major melody in the violins
sections.mNote: A long melody above moving basses

sections.label: C · March figures in wind and brass
sections.mNote: Short wind and brass figures break into the violin melody.

sections.label: B′ · Lyrical theme in C major
sections.mNote: The lyrical theme begins its first development.

sections.label: Dev · Funeral march with horn chorale
sections.mNote: Six horns play a hymn against the funeral march.

sections.label: A′ · C-minor march, reprise
sections.mNote: The low-string figures of the opening come back at full force

sections.label: B″ · E major returns, violins
sections.mNote: The long melody stays in the distant key.

sections.label: Coda · Funeral march, C minor
sections.mNote: C minor; broken phrases, then a descending close.

cues.title: First theme, cellos and basses
cues.text: Cellos and double basses play the first theme in C minor beneath tremolo in the upper strings. Their phrases break off and start again. Mahler marks the movement Allegro maestoso, with thoroughly serious and solemn expression.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement I, opening. The lower-string first subject and upper tremolo are also described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-1-allegro-maestoso/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s letter of 1896
cues.text: In a letter of 1896 Mahler described this movement as “the titanic struggles of a mighty being still caught in the toils of this world”, grappling with life and fate, and with “his death”. He had earlier called the movement Todtenfeier, funeral rites.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s letter of 1896 on the symphony, quoted by the Mahler Foundation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-manuscript/. The title Todtenfeier for the first movement, no later than October 1889: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score, https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Violin melody in E major
cues.text: At rehearsal 3 the violins play a long, connected melody in E major, marked “Im Tempo nachgeben”. Soft horns support it. The bass keeps moving below.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, p. 8, rehearsal 3: Im Tempo nachgeben, long violin melody, horns and moving low strings. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performance for Hans von Bülow, 1891
cues.text: In 1891 Mahler played the early version of this movement to Hans von Bülow at the piano, and Bülow covered his ears. At Bülow’s memorial service in Hamburg on 29 March 1894, Mahler heard the hymn that led him to the symphony’s choral finale.
cues.evidence: The piano performance and Bülow’s response are recorded in the Todtenfeier chronology: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/ . The memorial service was on 29 March 1894: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Second subject in C major
cues.text: The second subject opens the first development in C major. Winds and strings play it softly, and the harp plays figures between the phrases.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, pp. 14–17. The second subject’s C-major opening of the first development is identified at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-1-allegro-maestoso/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Todtenfeier” manuscript, Prague, 1888
cues.text: The title page of the earliest manuscript, dated Prague, 10 September 1888, reads “Todtenfeier”, Symphony in C minor, first movement. The title almost certainly comes from Siegfried Lipiner’s German translation of Mickiewicz’s Dziady, published in 1887.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score of Symphony No. 2 (December 2010). https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Mahler’s remark, summer 1893
cues.text: In the summer of 1893, when he resumed the symphony after five years, Mahler told Natalie Bauer-Lechner: “My two symphonies treat exhaustively my entire life; it is experience and suffering that I have written down with my lifeblood.”
cues.evidence: Natalie Bauer-Lechner’s recollection, quoted in Stephen E. Hefling’s essay for the Universal Edition study score (December 2010). https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Hans von Bülow, Hamburg, 1891
cues.text: In Hamburg in 1891 Mahler failed to persuade Hans von Bülow to perform Todtenfeier. According to the later recollection of Mahler’s friend Josef Foerster, Bülow said: “If that is still music, then I understand nothing about music anymore.”
cues.evidence: Josef Bohuslav Foerster, Gustav Mahler in Hamburg, Prager Presse, 16 April 1922, cited in Stephen E. Hefling’s essay for the Universal Edition study score. https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Second development, horn chorale
cues.text: The second development sets the march beside a solemn chorale for six horns. Its tune is related to the Dies irae, the old chant of the Day of Judgement. Similar hymn-like brass writing returns in the finale.
cues.evidence: The six-horn chorale, its Dies irae relationship and later role are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-1-allegro-maestoso/ . This note describes the second development as a whole.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second autograph score, 1894
cues.text: On 29 April 1894 Mahler completed a new autograph score of this movement, revising it before the symphony was finished. He signed off the autograph of the whole work in Hamburg on 18 December 1894.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation chronology of Symphony No. 2: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/. The Hamburg date: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score, https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Dissonant climax, bars 324–329
cues.text: The Dies irae chant is quoted from bar 270, and shortly afterwards the movement reaches a harshly dissonant climax at bars 324–329. Stephen Hefling noted that the finale later dissolves the approach to this same climax, well before the chorus proclaims redemption.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score: the Dies irae sequence from bar 270 and the climax at bars 324–329 of the revised movement. https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation of the first subject
cues.text: The music returns to C minor, and the low-string figures of the opening come back. The basses play in short, broken phrases, as at the start.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, recapitulation of the first subject; the existing section boundary places the returning march.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second subject returns in E major
cues.text: In the recapitulation the second subject returns in the violins in E major, the key of its first appearance. The strings play it broadly, with softer chords in the woodwind and horns.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, recapitulation of the second subject. Its return in the original E major is documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda in C minor
cues.text: The coda turns back towards C minor. After the violin melody, short string phrases, figures from the earlier wind parts and the march rhythms return.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, closing pages, pp. 49–56.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performances, Berlin, 1895
cues.text: Mahler conducted the first three movements in Berlin on 4 March 1895 and the whole symphony on 13 December. Most critics were dismissive or hostile. The audience’s enthusiasm grew through the evening and ended in a long ovation.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score (December 2010). https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Pause of at least five minutes
cues.text: On the last page Mahler asks for a pause of at least five minutes between the funeral march and the A♭-major dance that follows.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, p. 56: Hier folgt eine Pause von mindestens 5 Minuten. The instruction concerns the interval between movements.

transitions.title: Violins move to E major
transitions.from: A · March theme in cellos and basses
transitions.to: B · E major melody in the violins
transitions.how: At rehearsal 3 the music moves from the C-minor march into E major. The violins play a long melody over moving low strings, with soft horns and woodwind chords. The marking Im Tempo nachgeben tells the conductor to let the tempo yield with the phrase.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement I, p. 8, rehearsal 3.

transitions.title: The second subject returns to the march
transitions.from: B · E major melody in the violins
transitions.to: C · March figures in wind and brass
transitions.how: The E-major violin phrase of the second subject runs into shorter orchestral figures at rehearsal 3. Winds and brass sharpen the accents, and the low strings take up the march’s repeated movement again beneath them.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, the continuation after the second subject at rehearsal 3.

transitions.title: Development opens in C major
transitions.from: C · March figures in wind and brass
transitions.to: B′ · Lyrical theme in C major
transitions.how: The march dies away and the lyrical subject begins the development in C major. Wind phrases and strings extend the melody into longer spans, and the harps enter among the fading orchestral chords.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, pp. 14–17; C-major development described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-1-allegro-maestoso/

transitions.title: March and horn chorale in the second development
transitions.from: B′ · Lyrical theme in C major
transitions.to: Dev · Funeral march with horn chorale
transitions.how: The first development ends quietly, and the march returns. In the second development, short string figures and a measured chorale for six horns are heard together. The chorale’s longer notes are held across the march rhythms.
transitions.evidence: The movement’s two developments and six-horn chorale are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-1-allegro-maestoso/ . The established boundary covers the start of the second development, before the chorale’s full statement.

transitions.title: Return to the low strings
transitions.from: Dev · Funeral march with horn chorale
transitions.how: The central orchestral outburst breaks off. Cellos and basses play the opening figures again in C minor, with rests between the attacks as at the start. The march returns from these low strings.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, return of the first subject in the recapitulation.

transitions.title: Second subject returns in E major
transitions.how: The march music recedes. The violins take up their long melody again in E major, with restrained winds and horns around the line. The theme returns in its original key, a major third above the movement’s C.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, recapitulated E-major second subject.

transitions.title: The violin melody gives way to C minor
transitions.how: The violin melody breaks into fragments and C minor returns. The low strings take up the funeral rhythm again beneath short phrases in the winds. In the coda, winds and strings play a rapid descending scale, followed by the short closing chords (Hofmeister score, movement I, pp. 49–56; the descending close is on p. 56).
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement I, pp. 49–56; the descending close appears on p. 56.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: First movement, pp. 1–56: low-string opening, E-major violin theme at rehearsal 3 and descending scales on the final page.

timeline.note: Cellos and basses begin the march beneath trembling violins and violas.
Low strings play short phrases beneath the upper strings’ tremolo.
Violins play in E major above quiet horns, wind chords and moving low strings.
Quiet wind phrases and harp figures pass above sustained strings.
Cellos and basses return to the opening march figures in C minor.
The long violin melody returns, accompanied by quiet woodwind and horns.
Winds and strings run downwards; horns punctuate the descent before the short closing chords.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
